sec.title: Background
sec.p: Vobramitamab duocarmazine is an investigational antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) targeting B7 homolog 3 (B7‐H3) with a cytotoxic duocarmycin‐based DNA‐alkylating payload. This study evaluated its safety and antitumor activity in advanced solid tumors.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In this phase 1/2 trial (CP‐MGC‐018‐01/NCT03729596), vobramitamab duocarmazine was evaluated at 0.5–4.0 mg/kg intravenously every 3 weeks. The multicohort tumor‐expansion phase focused on metastatic castration‐resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), lung, breast, melanoma, and squamous head and neck carcinomas. Primary end points were safety and tolerability. Secondary end points included pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity, and antitumor activity.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Across vobramitamab duocarmazine–treated patients, 97.9% (140 of 143) experienced treatment‐related adverse events (TRAEs) of all grades; the grade ≥3 TRAE rate was 65.0% (93 of 143). With two dose‐limiting toxicities in patients receiving 4.0 mg/kg (grade 4 afebrile neutropenia and grade 3 fatigue), the recommended dose for expansion was 3.0 mg/kg. Among all patients treated at 3.0 mg/kg, the rate of grade ≥3 TRAEs was 65.3% (79 of 121) and the confirmed objective response rate (ORR) was 7.2% (seven of 97), with a 6.3‐month median duration of response (DOR). Among patients with mCRPC receiving 3.0 mg/kg, the confirmed ORR was 8.3% (two of 24), with a 5.3‐month median DOR; the confirmed prostate‐specific antigen with a ≥50% decline from the baseline response rate was 43.9% (18 of 41), with a 6.2‐month median DOR.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Vobramitamab duocarmazine demonstrated modest antitumor activity across tumor types, with the most pronounced activity in mCRPC. Treatment was limited by toxicity, particularly pleural effusions and fatigue, which restricted dosing duration. Study treatment was discontinued to refocus on mCRPC in a randomized phase 2 study (TAMARACK/NCT05551117), which was later discontinued after assessment of the vobramitamab duocarmazine safety and efficacy profile.

abstract.p: The safety and activity of vobramitamab duocarmazine (vobra duo), a novel investigational anti–B7 homolog 3 antibody–drug conjugate with a potent cytotoxic duocarmycin‐based DNA‐alkylating payload, were investigated in a phase 1/2 trial. Vobra duo demonstrated evidence of antitumor activity in patients with advanced/metastatic solid tumors, especially in metastatic castration‐resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), which led to the initiation of the mCRPC TAMARACK/NCT05551117 trial, which was later terminated because of toxicity.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) have emerged as a class of therapeutic agents for the targeted treatment of cancer. 1 ADCs combine the tumor target specificity of a monoclonal antibody with highly potent cytotoxic payloads for the selective delivery of cytotoxic agents to cancer cells. 1 The mechanism of action of ADCs offers the potential for increased efficacy, while minimizing drug exposure to healthy tissues, which thereby expands the therapeutic window of an otherwise intolerable toxin payload. 1

B7 homolog 3 (B7‐H3) is an immune checkpoint molecule highly expressed in multiple solid tumors, including prostate cancer, with limited expression in healthy tissue. 2 , 3 B7‐H3 may play an immune‐suppressive role in favor of cancer growth, which makes B7‐H3 a suitable target for targeted therapy. 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 In most cancers, overexpression of B7‐H3 is associated with multiple adverse clinical and pathologic features of disease, increased risk of recurrence, and reduced survival. 6 , 7

Vobramitamab duocarmazine (vobra duo) is a novel investigational anti–B7‐H3 ADC with a potent cytotoxic duocarmycin‐based DNA‐alkylating payload, delivered to dividing and nondividing B7‐H3–expressing cancer cells, while minimizing exposure to healthy tissues. 3 , 8

The objective of this dose‐escalation and cohort‐expansion phase 1/2 trial was to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity, and preliminary antitumor activity of vobra duo in patients with relapsed/refractory, unresectable locally advanced, or metastatic solid tumors, with a particular focus on metastatic castration‐resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC).

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This phase 1/2 open‐label, dose‐escalation, and multicohort tumor‐expansion clinical trial (CP‐MGC‐018‐01/NCT03729596) was designed to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity, and preliminary antitumor activity of vobra duo as monotherapy (Figure S1). In the dose‐escalation phase, vobra duo was evaluated with a 3 + 3 + 3 dose‐escalation design at doses ranging from 0.5 to 5.0 mg/kg intravenously (iv) every 3 weeks in successive cohorts (Figure S1). Throughout the study, vobra duo was administered as an iv infusion over the course of 60 min on days 1 and 22 of each 6‐week cycle; patients could receive up to 18 total cycles. During cohort expansion, patients with relapsed/refractory, unresectable mCRPC, metastatic non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), locally advanced or metastatic triple‐negative breast cancer (TNBC), locally advanced or metastatic melanoma, or metastatic or recurrent unresectable squamous cell cancer of head and neck (SCCHN) received vobra duo at the recommended dose for expansion (RDE) of 3.0 mg/kg iv every 3 weeks, established during dose escalation on the basis of review of the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics data (Figure S1). To manage toxicity, dose interruptions of up to 21 days and dose reductions were allowed.

sec.title: Patient eligibility
sec.p: Patients must have been aged ≥18 years and had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) of ≤2. Archival or formalin‐fixed, paraffin‐embedded tumor tissue had to be available to evaluate B7‐H3 immunohistochemistry (IHC), although B7‐H3 expression was not required for eligibility. In the escalation phase, eligible patients had relapsed/refractory, unresectable locally advanced, or metastatic solid tumors for which no therapy with demonstrated clinical benefit was available. For cohort expansion, patients with mCRPC were eligible if they had progressed during or after one prior line of chemotherapy for metastatic disease and no more than two prior lines of an antihormonal agent (e.g., abiraterone or enzalutamide) with a prostate‐specific antigen (PSA) value of at least 2 ng/mL. Patients with mCRPC were eligible if they met at least one of the following criteria: progression in measurable disease (Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors, version 1.1 [RECIST v1.1]); appearance of two or more new bone lesions according to Prostate Cancer Working Group 2 (PCWG2); and a rising PSA defined as at least two sequential rises in PSA measurements obtained ≥1 week apart above the reference value, which was the last PSA (≥2 ng/mL) measured before the first PSA rise as defined by PCWG2. Patients with mCRPC with bone‐only disease were allowed. Patients with metastatic NSCLC were eligible if they had failed standard cytotoxic, targeted, and biologic or checkpoint inhibitor therapy, with no more than two prior lines of cytotoxic chemotherapy. Patients with locally advanced or metastatic TNBC were eligible if they had progressed during or after at least one systemic therapy. Patients with SCCHN were eligible if they had progressed during or after at least one systemic therapy for metastatic or recurrent unresectable disease, with no more than two prior lines of cytotoxic chemotherapy. Patients with melanoma were eligible if they had progressed during or after at least one systemic treatment for unresectable locally advanced or metastatic disease, including patients who were intolerant of or refused standard therapy.

Patients were excluded if they had symptomatic central nervous system metastases or clinically significant cardiovascular or pulmonary disease, including pericardial or pleural effusions. Prior treatment with any systemic anticancer therapy, including systemic chemotherapy, biologic agents, investigational agents, or mediastinal/pelvic radiation within 4 weeks, small molecule–targeted or kinase inhibitors within 14 days, and B7‐H3–targeted agents, was not allowed. Prior therapy with a radioligand within 6 months in the mCRPC cohort expansion was not allowed.

sec.title: Ethics approval and patient consent to participate
sec.p: This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use Tripartite Guideline for Good Clinical Practice, including archiving of essential documents, and in compliance with other applicable regulatory requirements. Institutional review boards or independent ethics committees approved the protocol at each participating site. Patients provided written informed consent before enrollment.

sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: Primary objectives of the dose‐escalation phase were to evaluate the safety, dose‐limiting toxicities (DLTs), and maximum tolerated dose or maximum administered dose of vobra duo in patients with advanced solid tumors. Secondary objectives were the pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity, and antitumor activity of vobra duo. Primary objectives of the cohort‐expansion phase were the safety and tolerability of vobra duo. Secondary objectives were the antitumor activity of vobra duo 3.0 mg/kg in patients with mCRPC, NSCLC, TNBC, melanoma, and SCCHN, as well as radiographic progression‐free survival (rPFS), PSA response rate, and best PSA percent change in patients with mCRPC. Exploratory objectives included progression‐free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and the association of B7‐H3 expression with clinical response.

sec.title: Analysis populations
sec.p: The safety population included all patients in the dose‐escalation and dose‐expansion cohorts who received at least one dose of vobra duo. This population was used for baseline characteristics, safety, pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity, PFS, rPFS, and OS.

The response‐evaluable population included all patients who received at least one dose of vobra duo, had baseline measurable or nonmeasurable disease (for patients with mCRPC, only those with baseline‐measurable disease were included), and had at least one postbaseline radiographic tumor assessment or had discontinued treatment because of clinical progressive disease or death. This population was used for tumor assessment and analysis of response rates.

The PSA response‐evaluable population included patients with mCRPC, a baseline PSA of ≥2 ng/mL, and at least one postbaseline PSA measurement. This population was used for analysis of PSA response rates.

sec.title: Safety assessment
sec.p: Safety assessments were based on the evaluation of adverse events (AEs) that occurred from the time of initiation of vobra duo administration until 30 days after the last dose or until the start of a subsequent systemic anticancer therapy, if earlier. The severity of AEs was graded according to National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.03.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity assessment
sec.p: Serum concentrations of conjugated antibody and total antibody after administration of vobra duo were monitored via quantitative bioanalytic methods. Plasma concentrations of SYD986 (the activated drug also known as payload) after administration of vobra duo were monitored via a liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry assay.
The antidrug antibody (ADA) against vobra duo was detected via validated bridging assay methods.

sec.title: Efficacy assessment
sec.p: Tumor assessments were obtained via computed tomography and/or magnetic resonance imaging scans. For mCRPC, a bone scan was obtained in addition to computed tomography and/or magnetic resonance imaging scans at baseline and on study. Target and nontarget lesions were designated at screening and then evaluated every 6 weeks for the first four cycles and every other cycle thereafter for patients in dose escalation or every 9 weeks for patients in cohort expansion. At each on‐treatment tumor assessment time point, the objective response status was determined by the investigator according to RECIST v1.1. Patients in cohort expansion who discontinued study treatment were followed for survival status every 3 months for a 2‐year survival follow‐up period after the last vobra duo dose.

In patients with mCRPC, PSA was assessed every 6 weeks for the first four cycles and every 12 weeks thereafter; rPFS and PSA were assessed every 3 weeks via PCWG2 criteria. The PSA50 response rate was defined as a ≥50% decline from baseline in PSA with confirmation at least 3 weeks later.

sec.title: Biomarker assessment
sec.p: To explore the association with clinical response, B7‐H3 expression was assessed retrospectively by IHC on archival and fresh pretreatment tumor specimens. An IHC assay with the Spring Bioscience (Pleasanton, California) anti–B7‐H3 antibody (clone SP206) was developed on head and neck carcinoma and NSCLC VT0000020580 and S95‐7815, respectively, via VENTANA OptiView DAB detection on the VENTANA Benchmark ULTRA staining platform (Tucson, Arizona). Staining intensity was scored on a semiquantitative four‐integer scale from 0 (negative) to 3 (or 3+) by a certified anatomic pathologist. The percentage of cells staining positively at each intensity level was recorded. Scoring was based on the localization of B7‐H3 to the cell membrane and cytoplasma. The H score was calculated by combining components of staining intensity with the percentage of positive cells (range, 0–300). IHC positive was defined as cytoplasma H score >0 or membrane H score >0.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: AEs were summarized by their relationship to the study drug and by severity. Categorical data were summarized by the number and percentage of patients. Continuous variables were summarized by descriptive statistics. The two‐sided 95% exact binomial confidence intervals (CIs) of both the objective response rate (ORR) and PSA response rate were calculated. The Kaplan–Meier method was used to estimate the PFS, duration of response (DOR), OS, and rate of PSA50 response with duration at 6 months. The method of Brookmeyer and Crowley was used to construct the 95% CI for the median time of each time‐to‐event end point.

sec.title: Patient disposition
sec.p: As of August 3, 2023, overall, 143 patients received vobra duo in the dose‐escalation (n = 29) and cohort‐expansion phases (n = 114) (Table S1). A total of 121 patients received vobra duo 3.0 mg/kg every 3 weeks (the RDE): seven patients in dose escalation and 114 patients in cohort expansion (mCRPC, n = 41; NSCLC, n = 21; melanoma, n = 21; TNBC, n = 18; SCCHN, n = 13) (Table S1). All 121 patients discontinued; progressive disease (PD) was the most common cause of treatment discontinuation (n = 79), followed by AEs (n = 33), patient decision (n = 7), physician decision (n = 1), and death (n = 1).

sec.title: Baseline characteristics
sec.p: The median age of the overall safety population (N = 143) across the dose‐escalation and cohort‐expansion phases was 65 years (Table S2). These patients had received a median of three prior cancer therapies, and 44.1% (63 of 143) had metastatic disease at diagnosis (Table S2).

The median age of the patients treated with vobra duo 3.0 mg/kg (n = 121) was 66 years (Table 1). These patients had a median of three prior cancer therapies, 97.5% (118 of 121) of patients had an ECOG PS of 0 or 1, and 43.0% (52 of 121) had metastatic disease at diagnosis (Table 1).

sec.p: The median age of patients with mCRPC (n = 41) was 70 years (Table 1). Patients with mCRPC had a median of three prior cancer therapies, and the median baseline PSA was 99.0 ng/mL (Table 1).

sec.title: Exposure
sec.p: The median overall treatment duration of vobra duo in the overall safety population (N = 143) was 15.1 weeks (range, 1.1–68.1 weeks), with a median overall number of 1.5 cycles (range, 0.5–7.5 cycles) and a median overall dose intensity of 79.7% (range, 20.7%–138.4%) as a result of dose reductions/interruptions (Table 2). Among patients treated at the 3.0‐mg/kg dose, the median treatment duration was 16.1 weeks (range, 1.9–68.1 weeks), with a median number of 2.0 cycles (range, 0.5–7.5 cycles) and a median dose intensity of 75.1% (range, 20.7%–102.9%) (Table 2). Patients with mCRPC received a median of two cycles (which corresponded to four doses); patients in the other tumor cohorts received a median of 1.5 cycles (which corresponded to three doses) (Table 2).

sec.title: Safety in the overall safety population
sec.p: All patients in the overall safety population (N = 143) experienced at least one treatment‐emergent AE (TEAE), which were treatment related in 140 patients (97.9%) (Table S3). A total of 107 patients (74.8%) had grade ≥3 TEAEs, which were treatment related in 93 patients (65.0%). Treatment‐emergent serious AEs (TESAEs) occurred in 41.3% of patients, and treatment‐related serious AEs (TRSAEs) in 32.2%. Among the overall safety population, there were seven deaths (4.9%) within 30 days of the last dose, five (3.5%) of which were due to AEs.

sec.title: Safety in the dose‐escalation cohort
sec.p: Two DLTs occurred in the dose‐escalation cohort (n = 29). One patient receiving vobra duo 2.0 mg/kg experienced grade 4 afebrile neutropenia that led to treatment discontinuation; the event was considered nonserious by the investigator, definitely related to vobra duo, and resolved in 51 days. The other patient, who received vobra duo 4.0 mg/kg, experienced grade 3 fatigue that lasted >72 h and led to treatment discontinuation; the event was considered nonserious by the investigator, probably related to vobra duo, and resolved in 5 days. However, because of these two DLTs, the 5.0‐mg/kg dose was not administered. The maximum administered dose of vobra duo was 4.0 mg/kg every 3 weeks. The RDE of vobra duo was 3.0 mg/kg every 3 weeks.

sec.title: Safety in patients treated with vobra duo 3.0 mg/kg every 3 weeks
sec.p: All 121 patients treated at the 3.0‐mg/kg dose experienced at least one TEAE, which were treatment related in 120 patients (99.2%) (Table 3). A total of 88 patients (72.7%) had grade ≥3 TEAEs, which were treatment related in 79 patients (65.3%) (Table 3). TESAEs occurred in 43.0% of patients, and TRSAEs in 33.1% (Table 3). Among the 121 patients treated at the 3.0‐mg/kg dose, there were five deaths (4.1%) within 30 days of the last dose, four (3.3%) of which were due to AEs. Specifically, one patient with mCRPC died of treatment‐related disseminated intravascular coagulation, one patient with mCRPC died of treatment‐related cardiac arrest, one patient with TNBC died of treatment‐related hepatic failure, and one patient with mCRPC died of coronavirus disease 2019—an event deemed not treatment related (Table 3).

sec.p: TEAEs leading to vobra duo discontinuation occurred in 34 patients (28.1%): four in the 3.0‐mg/kg dose‐escalation cohort, 15 in the mCRPC cohort, five in the NSCLC cohort, five in the TNBC cohort, four in the melanoma cohort, and one in the SCCHN cohort (Table 3). TEAEs leading to dose reductions occurred in 28.6% of patients in the 3.0‐mg/kg dose‐escalation cohort and in patients with mCRPC (68.3%), NSCLC (47.6%), TNBC (33.3%), melanoma (52.4%), and SCCHN (46.2%) (Table 3). TEAEs leading to dose interruptions (including infusion interruption and dose delay) occurred in 71.4% of patients in the 3.0‐mg/kg dose‐escalation cohort and in patients with mCRPC (68.3%), NSCLC (61.9%), TNBC (55.6%), melanoma (85.7%), and SCCHN (53.8%) (Table 3).

The most common TRAEs of all grades (reported by ≥25% of patients) were fatigue (48.8%), palmar–plantar erythrodysesthesia (PPE) syndrome (42.1%), neutropenia (37.2%), pleural effusion (32.2%), nausea (30.6%), decreased appetite (27.3%), peripheral edema (27.3%), and anemia (25.6%) (Table 4). The most common TRAEs of grade ≥3 (reported by ≥10% of patients) were neutropenia (26.4%) and thrombocytopenia (9.9%) (Table S4). The most common TRSAEs (reported by ≥3 patients) were pleural effusion (7.4%), anemia and atrial fibrillation (4.1% each), pericardial effusion and abdominal pain (3.3% each), and thrombocytopenia, diarrhea, urinary tract infection, and acute kidney injury (2.5% each).

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity
sec.p: Vobra duo ADC, total antibody, and SYD986 demonstrated predictable pharmacokinetics (secondary end point), with dose‐proportional serum concentrations over time between doses of 0.5 and 4.0 mg/kg iv (Figure S2).
A total of 140 participants had baseline ADA data available, all of whom were negative (Table S7). Of these, 14 (10.0%) were positive at least once after baseline, with titers ranging from 15 to 120.

sec.title: Clinical activity
sec.p: Among 115 response‐evaluable patients, the confirmed best overall response per investigator assessment, based on RECIST v1.1, was partial response (PR) in eight patients (7.0%), stable disease in 60 patients (52.2%), and PD in 41 patients (35.7%). Overall, the confirmed ORR was 7.0%, and the median DOR was 6.3 months (95% CI, 4.27 months to not estimable) (Table S8).

Among the 21 response‐evaluable patients in the dose‐escalation phase, the confirmed ORR was 4.8% (95% CI, 0.1%–23.8%; one of 21), which ranged from 0% (in the 0.5‐, 1.0‐, 2.0‐, and 3.0‐mg/kg cohorts) to 25.0% (in the 4.0‐mg/kg cohort) (Figure S3; Table S8).
Among the 97 response‐evaluable patients treated at the 3.0‐mg/kg dose, the confirmed ORR was 7.2%, which ranged from 0% (in the TNBC cohort) to 15.0% (in the NSCLC cohort) (Table 5).

In the mCRPC cohort, there were 24 RECIST v1.1 response‐evaluable patients with measurable disease at baseline (shown in this table) and 17 with nonmeasurable disease at baseline (not shown in this table); of the 17 patients with nonmeasurable disease at baseline, 14 had bone‐only disease.
Among these 97 patients, there were three who were treated at the 3.0‐mg/kg dose in the dose‐escalation phase (shown in Table S8).

sec.p: Among the 24 response‐evaluable patients with mCRPC, six had PR: two confirmed PR and four unconfirmed PR. The confirmed ORR was 8.3% (95% CI, 1.0%–27.0%; two of 24), and the median DOR was 5.3 months (95% CI, 4.27 months to not applicable) (Figure 1A,B; Table 5). The confirmed PSA50 response rate was 43.9% (95% CI, 28.5%–60.1%; 18 of 41), and the median duration of PSA50 response was 6.2 months (95% CI, 2.07–10.02 months) (Figure 1C).

sec.p: Among the 114 patients in the cohort expansion, the median PFS ranged from 2.4 months (TNBC) to 5.5 months (mCRPC) (Table S9). Additional efficacy data in the other expansion cohorts are described in Table 5, Table S9, Figure S4 (NSCLC), Figure S5 (TNBC), Figure S6 (melanoma), and Figure S7 (SCCHN). Clinical responses did not appear to correlate with baseline B7‐H3 expression in tumor samples (Figure 1B,C; Figures S4–S7).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: In this phase 1 trial, vobra duo 3.0 mg/kg every 3 weeks demonstrated modest antitumor activity in multiple tumor types, particularly mCRPC. The confirmed ORR was 7.2% (seven of 97) across all patients treated at 3.0 mg/kg, and 8.3% (two of 24) in the mCRPC cohort. However, high rates of vobra duo dose modifications as a result of AEs were observed, and discontinuations were frequently reported: 28.1% (34 of 121) of patients treated at 3.0 mg/kg, and 36.6% (15 of 41) in the mCRPC cohort. This study was terminated in April 2023, before the completion of all expansion cohorts, as mCRPC became the primary focus for subsequent clinical development. This decision followed the encouraging activity of vobra duo in mCRPC, which demonstrated a median PFS of 5.5 months and a median OS of 12.3 months. In addition, 43.9% (18 of 41) of patients with mCRPC were PSA responders, with a median DOR of 6.2 months. The sponsor elected to focus on mCRPC for dose optimization in a subsequent study (TAMARACK) before pursuing other indications, with the hope of identifying a more tolerable dose and schedule.

Other ADCs targeting B7‐H3 are under investigation in mCRPC. DB‐1311/BNT324 showed encouraging results in a phase 1/2 trial (NCT05914116) in 73 patients with mCRPC, with a confirmed ORR of 30.8%, a median rPFS not reached, and a 6‐month rPFS of 67.7%. 9 Although rates of treatment discontinuation as a result of TRAEs were low (9.6%) in the mCRPC cohort, rates of grade ≥3 TRAEs were reported in 42.5% of patients with mCRPC, mainly hematologic and gastrointestinal events. 9 Ifinatamab deruxtecan has also demonstrated promising results, with a confirmed ORR of 25.4% and a median rPFS of 5.3 months in 73 patients with mCRPC in a phase 1/2 trial (NCT04145622). 10 Treatment discontinuations as a result of TEAEs were low (4.0%) but rates of grade ≥3 TEAEs were reported in 46.7% of the mCRPC cohort. 10 A phase 3 trial of ifinatamab deruxtecan for mCRPC is ongoing (NCT06925737). MHB088C is another B7‐H3–targeted ADC that has shown promising results in a phase 1/2 trial (CTR20231298) conducted in 47 patients with mCRPC. 11 MHB088C demonstrated preliminary antitumor activity, with an ORR of 7.5%, a disease control rate of 95.0%, and a 6‐month rPFS of 81.1%. 11 Treatment discontinuations as a result of TRAEs were low (2.1%) but the rate of grade ≥3 TRAEs was 57.4%. 11 Moreover, the B7‐H3 ADC YL201 has demonstrated promising efficacy and an acceptable safety profile in a phase 1 trial of patients with advanced solid tumors, 12 and is currently under evaluation in a phase 2 trial for patients with mCRPC (NCT06241846).

Compared with other B7‐H3–targeted agents, vobra duo exhibited a distinct toxicity profile, with pleural and pericardial effusions of moderate to high intensity being a main concern, and treatment‐limiting PPE syndrome being a significant concern as well. Among other B7‐H3–targeting ADCs, hematologic toxicities seen with vobra duo were consistent and treatment limiting, as in other cases. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 Vobra duo effusions may be driven by its potent DNA‐alkylating payload, with possible release of the cytotoxic payload into the systemic circulation causing off‐target toxicity. 13 , 14 Effusions triggered by vobra duo could alternatively be a type of cytokine release syndrome with immune activation, given that other antibody‐based therapies can trigger these events in various cancers, including prostate cancer. 14 , 15 The metabolism of duocarmycin occurs by conjugation to glutathione 16 , 17 , 18 ; notably, pleural effusions have been reported to be associated with glutathione depletion in the autoimmune disease lupus erythematosus. 19 , 20 Therefore, the effusions triggered by vobra duo may have a potential autoimmune nature. The protocol recommended observation for grade 1 pleural/pericardial effusion, and glucocorticoids were recommended for high‐grade AEs. Most of the effusions were low grade, and only five patients who reexperienced an effusion were treated with glucocorticoids; therefore, it remains unclear to what extent steroid treatment provided a benefit.

In this phase 1 trial, the median number of vobra duo doses administered was relatively low (three doses overall; four doses in patients with mCRPC) because of the dose reductions/interruptions necessary to manage toxicities. Therefore, lowering the starting dose and/or extending the interdose period may improve tolerability, extend treatment duration, and maintain or enhance the efficacy of vobra duo. To explore this possibility, the randomized phase 2 TAMARACK trial (NCT05551117) was designed. In TAMARACK, two alternative starting dosing schedules (2.0 and 2.7 mg/kg every 4 weeks) at lower doses and with a longer dosing interval compared with the phase 1 trial were assessed to mitigate toxicities and optimize the total number of doses administered and overall treatment duration in patients with mCRPC. The TAMARACK study was later terminated on the basis of sponsor assessment of the vobra duo safety and efficacy profile.

This phase 1 study is limited by its small sample size and the absence of a control arm. Moreover, the evaluable population in the mCRPC cohort was relatively small, given that patients with no measurable disease at baseline were excluded from response assessment. Although the sponsor does not plan to pursue further internal development of vobra duo, future directions for the development of this agent may require the use of an alternative linker and/or consideration of alternative tumor types beyond mCRPC. For instance, vobra duo exerted relevant antitumor activity in preclinical B7‐H3–expressing neuroblastoma models, and represents a potential candidate for clinical translation. 21
In conclusion, vobra duo demonstrated pronounced antitumor activity in mCRPC; however, treatment was limited by toxicity, and the phase 1 trial was terminated.
